items.prompt: What is the single most defining feature that sets mammals apart from all other animals?

options.label: They are warm-blooded.
options.feedback: Being warm-blooded is shared with birds, so it does not set mammals apart from all other animals.

options.label: They give birth to live young.
options.feedback: Some mammals, like the platypus, lay eggs, and some reptiles and fish also give birth to live young, so this is not unique to mammals.

options.label: They produce milk to feed their young.
options.feedback: Exactly. All mammals, without exception, nurse their young with milk produced by mammary glands—this is the defining trait.

options.label: They have hair on their bodies.
options.feedback: While most mammals have hair, some, like whales, have very little, and hair is not present in all mammals at all life stages, so it is not the single defining feature.

items.ok_line: Milk production is the hallmark of every mammal.
items.ko_line: Other traits are shared with other animal groups.
items.exp_text: The only feature every mammal shares is the ability to produce milk from mammary glands to feed its young. This is true for egg-laying monotremes like the platypus, marsupials like kangaroos, and placental mammals like humans. Warm-bloodedness is shared with birds, live birth occurs in some non-mammals, and hair is reduced or absent in some whales.

items.prompt: Which part of a mammal's body is covered by a layer of skin that contains hair follicles?

options.label: The entire body surface
options.feedback: Yes. Hair grows from follicles in the skin across the whole body, though density varies—whales have very little, while a fur seal has a dense coat.

options.label: Only the head and back
options.feedback: Hair can grow on the face, limbs, and belly too, not just the head and back, so this is too limited.

options.label: Only the limbs and tail
options.feedback: Limbs and tail are not the only hairy parts; the trunk and head also have hair follicles.

options.label: Only the neck and chest
options.feedback: Hair is not confined to the neck and chest; it appears all over the body in most mammals.

items.ok_line: Hair follicles cover the entire skin.
items.ko_line: Hair grows on all body regions.
items.exp_text: Mammals have hair follicles in the skin over their entire body. Some species, like the fur seal, have extremely dense fur, while others like the elephant have very sparse hair, but the follicles are there. This is universal among mammals, even if the hair is barely visible.

items.prompt: What is the name of the milk-producing glands that give the class Mammalia its name?

options.label: Sebaceous glands
options.feedback: Sebaceous glands produce an oily substance for skin and hair, not milk.

options.label: Mammary glands
options.feedback: Correct. Mammary glands are the modified sweat glands that produce milk, and 'Mammalia' comes from 'mamma,' the Latin word for breast.

options.label: Sweat glands
options.feedback: Sweat glands secrete sweat for cooling, not milk.

options.label: Scent glands
options.feedback: Scent glands produce chemicals for marking territory, not milk.

items.exp_text: Mammary glands are specialized glands in the skin that produce milk to nourish newborns. They are found in all female mammals and are the origin of the name 'Mammalia.' Sebaceous, sweat, and scent glands are separate and serve other purposes like lubrication, cooling, and communication.

items.prompt: Which of these is a mammal that lays eggs instead of giving birth to live young?

options.label: Kangaroo
options.feedback: Kangaroos give birth to tiny live young that crawl into a pouch, so they do not lay eggs.

options.label: Dolphin
options.feedback: Dolphins are placental mammals and give birth to live calves, not eggs.

options.label: Bat
options.feedback: Bats are placental mammals and give birth to live pups, not eggs.

options.label: Platypus
options.feedback: Yes. The platypus is a monotreme, a mammal that lays leathery eggs and then nurses the hatchlings with milk.

items.ko_line: These mammals give birth to live young.
items.exp_text: Monotremes—the platypus and the echidna—are the only mammals that lay eggs. After hatching, the young drink milk from the mother's mammary glands. Kangaroos, dolphins, and bats all give birth to live young, as they are marsupials or placental mammals.

items.prompt: What is the term for mammals that carry their young in a pouch after birth?

options.label: Marsupials
options.feedback: Correct. Marsupials like kangaroos, koalas, and opossums give birth to very undeveloped young that continue growing in a pouch.

options.label: Monotremes
options.feedback: Monotremes lay eggs and do not have pouches; they are a separate group.

options.label: Placentals
options.feedback: Placentals develop young fully inside the mother with a placenta; they do not use pouches.

options.label: Amphibians
options.feedback: Amphibians are not mammals at all; they are frogs and salamanders.

items.exp_text: Marsupials give birth to very small, underdeveloped young that crawl into the mother's pouch, where they attach to a teat and continue developing. This is different from monotremes, which lay eggs, and placentals, which keep the young inside the uterus for a long time.

items.prompt: What do all mammals have in their necks, regardless of species?

options.label: Four neck bones
options.feedback: Most mammals have more than four neck bones; that number is typical of some birds, not mammals.

options.label: Ten neck bones
options.feedback: Ten is not the standard number; it is too many for most mammals.

options.label: Seven neck bones
options.feedback: Right. Almost every mammal, from a giraffe to a mouse, has exactly seven cervical vertebrae, even if the bones vary greatly in length.

options.label: No neck bones, only muscle
options.feedback: All mammals have a skeleton that includes neck vertebrae; the neck is not just muscle.

items.ko_line: The number is fixed at seven.
items.exp_text: All mammals, whether a tiny shrew or a long-necked giraffe, have exactly seven cervical vertebrae in their neck. The giraffe's vertebrae are just very long, while a whale's are short and nearly fused, but the count remains seven. This is a shared skeletal feature of the class.

items.prompt: Which body system in mammals uses a four-chambered heart to pump blood?

options.label: Respiratory system
options.feedback: The respiratory system handles breathing and gas exchange, not pumping blood.

options.label: Circulatory system
options.feedback: Correct. The circulatory system includes the heart and blood vessels; mammals have a four-chambered heart that separates oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

options.label: Digestive system
options.feedback: The digestive system processes food, not blood circulation.

options.label: Nervous system
options.feedback: The nervous system controls the body with nerves, not blood flow.

items.ko_line: That system has a different job.
items.exp_text: Mammals have a four-chambered heart—two atria and two ventricles—that pumps blood through the circulatory system. This design keeps oxygen-rich blood separate from oxygen-poor blood, enabling high-energy activity. Reptiles and amphibians have three-chambered hearts, but birds also have four chambers like mammals.

items.prompt: What is the hard, protective outer layer of a mammal's tooth called?

options.label: Pulp
options.feedback: Pulp is the inner soft tissue with nerves and blood vessels, not the hard outer layer.

options.label: Dentin
options.feedback: Dentin is the hard substance beneath the enamel, but it is not the outermost layer.

options.label: Cementum
options.feedback: Cementum covers the root of a tooth, not the visible crown.

options.label: Enamel
options.feedback: Yes. Enamel is the hardest substance in the body and covers the crown of a tooth, protecting it from wear and decay.

items.ko_line: Those are internal or root coverings.
items.exp_text: The outer surface of a mammal's tooth crown is covered by enamel, the hardest material in the body. Underneath is dentin, and inside is pulp. Cementum surrounds the root. Enamel resists the wear from chewing food and is especially thick in grazing animals that grind abrasive plants.

items.prompt: Which sense is typically the most developed in mammals that are active at night, such as owls do not count?

options.label: Hearing
options.feedback: Correct. Many nocturnal mammals, like bats and mice, rely heavily on acute hearing to navigate and find prey in the dark.

options.label: Sight
options.feedback: Nocturnal mammals often have poor vision in the dark; they depend more on hearing and smell.

options.label: Taste
options.feedback: Taste helps with food selection but is not the primary sense for nighttime activity.

options.label: Touch
options.feedback: Touch is important, especially with whiskers, but hearing is the key sense for many nocturnal mammals.

items.ko_line: Those are less relied upon at night.
items.exp_text: Mammals active at night often have exceptional hearing, since sound works well in darkness. Bats use echolocation, and many small rodents have large ears to catch high-frequency sounds. Sight is often not the main sense at night, and taste and touch play secondary roles.

items.prompt: What is the name of the structure that connects a developing mammal to its mother's blood supply?

options.label: Umbilical cord
options.feedback: The umbilical cord is the rope-like structure, but the organ that attaches to the mother's uterus is the placenta.

options.label: Yolk sac
options.feedback: The yolk sac provides food in egg-laying animals; it is not the main connection in placental mammals.

options.label: Placenta
options.feedback: Right. The placenta is an organ that attaches to the mother's uterine lining and exchanges nutrients, oxygen, and waste between mother and fetus.

options.label: Amniotic sac
options.feedback: The amniotic sac is the fluid-filled bag that cushions the fetus, not the nutrient-exchange organ.

items.exp_text: In placental mammals, the placenta is the organ that connects the fetus to the mother's blood supply. It allows oxygen and nutrients to pass from mother to fetus while removing waste. The umbilical cord is the connection from fetus to placenta, but the placenta itself is the exchange site. Yolk sac and amniotic sac serve other purposes.
